# Abstract

This gazetteer compiles coordinates, spatial scopes and post-colonial population trajectories for 1.592 individually assessed settlements across 18 countries between 1960AD and 2025AD. Screened from 1.676 candidate municipal towns, mining centres, river ports and suburban agglomerations (84 excluded), the retained entries cover 1.208 cities across the seven core Central African republics alongside 384 settlements in adjacent cross-border buffer zones. Active interpolated series expand from 258 settlements at 1960AD to 367 at 1980AD, 519 at 2000AD, 1.356 at 2020AD and 1.308 at 2025AD, documenting urban growth from Kinshasa (11,94M agglomeration), Luanda (10,2M agglomeration), Yaoundé (5,46M agglomeration), Douala (4,11M agglomeration) and Lubumbashi (3,92M agglomeration) down to secondary interior market towns.



# Background

Tracking post-colonial urbanisation across Central Africa, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Angola requires reconciling official national census towns with contiguous built-up satellite footprints [@INE2016AngolaRGPH; @BUCREP2010CameroonRGPH; @OECD2024Africapolis]. Whereas Cameroon, the Republic of the Congo, Gabon and Angola (since 2014AD) conducted multi-round population censuses, the Democratic Republic of the Congo has held no completed national enumeration since July 1984 [@Shapiro2017FertilityEthnicity; @Dimbuene2023HighRisk]. Combining municipal census records with built-up agglomeration series resolves administrative under-bounding at rapidly expanding capitals while preserving city-proper series for historical comparison [@Lawunda2023PrivatisationLeau; @Monono2023TheChallenges].

# Methodology

## Candidate Screening and Scope Classification

Entries were screened across national statistical directories, UN demographic abstracts and Africapolis 2024AD urban polygons [@OECD2024Africapolis; @INE2016AngolaRGPH; @BUCREP2010CameroonRGPH]. From 1.676 initial candidates bounded across 5.286.992 km² and geoBoundaries national outlines [@Runfola2020GeoBoundaries], 84 duplicate alias records were removed, leaving 1.592 entries across 7.171 dated observations. Each row explicitly distinguishes municipal city-proper records (1.565 entries) from metropolitan agglomerations (27 entries).

## Country-Level Summary and Tabular Conventions

Table \ref{tab:country-gazetteer-summary} summarises site counts, municipal versus metropolitan scopes, total observations and active urban counts across each of the seven core republics and the external border buffer. Subsequent tables present linearly interpolated populations at five benchmark dates (1960AD, 1980AD, 2000AD, 2020AD and 2025AD) alongside each entry's peak value and year, marking dates outside observed spans with a hyphen (-).

# Testing and Validation

Rank-size regression across the upper 180 urban centres yields $q = 1,08$ ($R^2 = 0,98$), and full-sample fitting across all 1.592 entries yields $q = 1,2$ ($R^2 = 0,93$). Spatially deduplicating municipal and metropolitan duplicates leaves 1.529 distinct urban peaks in Figure \ref{fig:settlements-rank}, following a near-Zipf distribution ($q = 1,02$, $R^2 = 0,99$) [@OECD2024Africapolis].

# Results

## Democratic Republic of the Congo

Because the Congolese ledger contains 662 assessed settlements, Tables \ref{tab:cod-west}, \ref{tab:cod-south} and \ref{tab:cod-east-north} partition the national hierarchy into Western DR Congo (194 entries led by Kinshasa, Matadi, Kikwit and Mbandaka), South-Central DR Congo (249 entries led by Lubumbashi, Mbuji-Mayi, Kolwezi and Kananga) and Eastern and Northern DR Congo (219 entries led by Goma, Bukavu, Kisangani and Butembo) [@Shapiro2017FertilityEthnicity; @Martin2014MortalityRates; @Lawunda2023PrivatisationLeau].

# Limitations

Three caveats govern these tables. First, municipal (*City*) and built-up (*Metro*) entries coexist for major capitals such as Kinshasa, Luanda, Yaoundé, Douala, Brazzaville and Bangui and must not be summed together without scope filtering [@OECD2024Africapolis]. Second, post-2000AD Africapolis detections add many rapidly growing towns whose earlier colonial-era populations were unrecorded, producing hyphenated pre-2000AD cells. Third, combined settlement sums reflect urban footprints rather than full provincial populations, which are reported in the companion review.

# Conclusion

Taken together, these 1.592 individually assessed settlements trace the transformation of post-colonial Central Africa from scattered mid-century administrative stations to multi-million coastal and riverine metropolises between 1960AD and 2025AD.
